questions.question: A team lets Claude Code carry out a large refactor across many files over several days. Some steps run a codemod through shell commands that rewrites files Claude never edited itself, and a subagent also edits files. The team needs a dependable way to undo any single bad step later and to give reviewers a readable history of the changes. What should they rely on?

options.label: A
options.text: Have the agent copy each file to a backup folder before editing it and delete the copies once the refactor is merged

options.label: B
options.text: Treat the saved conversation transcript as the change record and resume the same session each day to review what changed

options.label: C
options.text: Commit each step to a Git branch as its own small commit, and treat those commits as the record of the refactor

options.label: D
options.text: Rely on /rewind checkpoints, which capture every file change the session makes, including shell-command and subagent edits

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect. Ad hoc backup copies depend on the agent remembering to make them, cannot capture files rewritten by shell commands outside its edits, and leave reviewers with no commit history. They recreate a weaker, manual version of what version control already provides. B: Incorrect. A transcript records what was said and done in one conversation, not a revertible snapshot of the repository, and it is not something reviewers can diff or merge. It also cannot undo a bad step, so it does not provide the rollback or shared history the team needs. C: Correct. The checkpointing documentation says files changed only by Bash commands are not tracked and must be reverted with version control such as Git, that subagent edits are likewise reverted with Git, and that Git provides the permanent history and collaboration that checkpoints do not. Small commits on a branch give a durable rollback point per step and a readable history for reviewers. D: Incorrect. Checkpoints are session-level recovery only: files changed solely by shell commands are not tracked, most subagent edits are not captured, and snapshots are deleted after a retention period. They are documented as not a replacement for version control, and they give reviewers no shared history.

questions.question: A plugin maintainer ships internal-tools, which declares the dependency { "name": "secrets-vault", "version": "~2.1.0" }. The secrets-vault plugin is git-backed, its marketplace entry points at 3.0.0, and its repository carries release tags for 2.1.0, 2.1.4, 2.2.0 and 3.0.0. Engineers also have report-gen installed, which constrains the same dependency with >=2.1. Select three statements that correctly describe how Claude Code handles secrets-vault in this setup.

options.label: A
options.text: Auto-update installs the 2.2.0 tag, because the looser >=2.1 range from report-gen takes priority over the stricter ~2.1.0 range from internal-tools

options.label: B
options.text: Uninstalling only report-gen frees secrets-vault to move to 3.0.0 on the next update, because the looser >=2.1 range was the one holding it back

options.label: C
options.text: Auto-update moves secrets-vault to the 2.1.4 tag, not to 2.2.0 or 3.0.0, because the installed dependency must satisfy both plugins' ranges at once

options.label: D
options.text: Installing a third plugin that requires ~3.0 of secrets-vault fails because no version satisfies every range, and existing installs stay unchanged

options.label: E
options.text: If both plugins are uninstalled but secrets-vault stays installed, it is no longer range-constrained and tracks its marketplace entry again

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect. Auto-update must satisfy every installed plugin's range, not the loosest one. The stricter ~2.1.0 range excludes 2.2.0, so a looser range from another plugin cannot widen what is allowed. B: Incorrect. internal-tools still constrains secrets-vault to ~2.1.0 after report-gen is removed, so the dependency remains held to that range and does not move to 3.0.0. Only removing every plugin that constrains it lifts the restriction. C: Correct. Auto-update fetches a constrained dependency at the highest git tag that satisfies every installed plugin's range. The overlap of the two ranges is 2.1.0 up to, but not including, 2.2.0, so 2.1.4 is the highest qualifying tag and the marketplace's latest version is ignored. D: Correct. A ~3.0 range does not overlap the ~2.1.0 range already imposed by internal-tools, so installing the third plugin fails with a conflicting version requirements message while the existing plugins and the dependency stay as they were. E: Correct. Once the last plugin that constrains a dependency is uninstalled, the dependency is no longer constrained to a version range and resumes tracking its marketplace entry on the next update.

questions.question: A platform team is hardening its MCP configuration for a customer-facing agent. Which of the following configuration choices correctly follow documented guidance for authentication and tool access control over MCP? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A
options.text: Configuring every MCP server the team has ever evaluated in mcpServers and setting allowedTools: ["mcp__*"] so the agent always has maximum optionality regardless of the task at hand

options.label: B
options.text: For a remote HTTP MCP server, placing a bearer token in the headers field of the server configuration rather than appending it to the URL as a query parameter

options.label: C
options.text: Passing the GitHub token through the stdio server's env field (GITHUB_TOKEN: process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN) rather than embedding it directly in the command string

options.label: D
options.text: Relying on permissionMode: "acceptEdits" to auto-approve MCP tool calls, since accept-edits mode is documented as covering both file edits and MCP tool execution

options.label: E
options.text: Using allowedTools: ["mcp__github__*"] to auto-approve every tool from a specific, deliberately chosen server, rather than reaching for permissionMode: "bypassPermissions" to unblock MCP calls generally

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect. Configuring every evaluated server and wildcard-approving all MCP tools maximizes both context-window cost and attack surface; this contradicts the guidance to scope allowedTools to the specific servers a task actually needs, and an unanchored wildcard like mcp__* in allowedTools is documented to be ignored with a startup warning rather than granting broad access. B: Correct. The documented pattern for HTTP/SSE authentication is passing headers such as Authorization: Bearer <token> in the server config's headers field, not embedding secrets in the URL. C: Correct. The documented pattern for stdio server authentication is passing credentials through the env field so they aren't hardcoded into the command or args. D: Incorrect. The documentation explicitly states permissionMode: "acceptEdits" does not auto-approve MCP tools; it only covers file edits and filesystem Bash commands, so relying on it for MCP access control is a documented anti-pattern. E: Correct. The documentation explicitly recommends preferring allowedTools wildcards for a specific MCP server over bypassPermissions, since bypassPermissions auto-approves MCP tools but also disables other safety prompts more broadly than necessary.

questions.question: A team building a Claude Code agent wants their custom database MCP tool to run without permission prompts, but they do not want to disable other safety prompts elsewhere in the agent. Which approach achieves this?

options.label: A
options.text: Set permissionMode to "bypassPermissions" for the entire session

options.label: B
options.text: Set permissionMode to "acceptEdits" so MCP calls are approved automatically

options.label: C
options.text: Add the specific tool name, such as "mcp__db__query", to allowedTools

options.label: D
options.text: Remove the tool from the "tools" array so Claude always asks before calling it

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect. bypassPermissions does approve MCP tools, but it also disables other safety prompts across the session, which is broader than intended. B: Incorrect. acceptEdits only auto-approves file edits and filesystem Bash commands; it does not auto-approve MCP tool calls. C: Correct. Listing the exact MCP tool name in allowedTools auto-approves only that tool, scoping the exception narrowly instead of disabling broader safety checks. D: Incorrect. Omitting a tool from "tools" removes it from Claude's context entirely, so Claude cannot call it at all rather than being prompted for approval.

questions.question: A team is building a public-facing chatbot and wants to pre-screen user messages for jailbreak attempts before they reach the main conversation, without adding significant latency or cost. Which approach best fits this goal?

options.label: A
options.text: Route each user message through a lightweight model call, such as Claude Haiku 4.5, constrained with structured outputs to return a simple harmful/not-harmful classification

options.label: B
options.text: Store a denylist of banned words and reject any message containing one of those words before it is ever sent to a model for classification

options.label: C
options.text: Require users to complete a CAPTCHA before every message so that only verified humans can submit prompts to the chatbot

options.label: D
options.text: Send every user message through the same large model used for the main conversation twice, once to classify intent and once to generate the actual reply

questions.explanation: A: Correct. A harmlessness screen using a lightweight model with structured output constraints is the pattern Anthropic recommends for fast, low-cost pre-screening of user input. B: Incorrect. Static keyword denylists are easily evaded through paraphrasing and do not generalize to novel jailbreak phrasing the way a model-based screen does. C: Incorrect. A CAPTCHA verifies that a request came from a human but does nothing to detect jailbreak or injection content within that human's message. D: Incorrect. Running the full large model twice per message doubles cost and latency without the efficiency benefit a lightweight screening model provides.

questions.question: A data protection officer is evaluating which privacy controls apply to a planned Claude API integration that will occasionally use the Files API and the code execution tool alongside standard Messages API calls. Which of the following statements accurately reflect Anthropic's documented data retention behavior? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A
options.text: Where Anthropic retains data to make a feature work, that retained data is never used for model training without the customer's express permission.

options.label: B
options.text: Enabling ZDR for one organization under an account automatically extends zero data retention to all other organizations under that same account, since ZDR is configured at the account level rather than per organization.

options.label: C
options.text: Under a ZDR arrangement, the Files API and code execution tool can still be used, but they are stateful features, so the data they process is not covered by ZDR.

options.label: D
options.text: Even under ZDR or HIPAA arrangements, Anthropic may retain data required by law, and may keep inputs and outputs flagged by its trust and safety systems for up to 2 years.

options.label: E
options.text: The Files API is eligible for ZDR because uploaded files are held only in memory during processing and are never persisted to storage, so data processed via this API falls under zero retention policies.

questions.explanation: A: Correct. Anthropic's documented commitment for features that necessarily retain data is that retained data is never used for model training without the customer's express permission. This statement is about training use, not about whether data is retained, so it does not conflict with the separate legal and flagged-content retention rules described in the flagged-content statement. B: Incorrect. ZDR is enabled per organization: each new organization requires ZDR to be enabled separately by the account team, and enablement does not automatically extend to other organizations under the same account. C: Correct. Nothing blocks a request that uses the Files API or code execution tool under a ZDR arrangement, but Anthropic documents these features as not ZDR-eligible because they are fundamentally stateful: the Files API stores your files and code execution runs in persistent containers. Using them is a choice to step outside ZDR for that specific data. 'Allowed' and 'not eligible' therefore describe the same fact: the request works, but ZDR does not protect the data it processes. D: Correct. The documented 'Retention regardless of arrangement' rule says that even with ZDR or HIPAA in place, Anthropic may retain data where required by law or where its automated trust and safety systems have flagged it, and a flagged chat or session may have its inputs and outputs retained for up to 2 years. This concerns how long data may be retained, not whether it may be used for training, so it is compatible with the training commitment in the other correct statement. E: Incorrect. The Files API is marked not eligible for ZDR: uploaded files are stored until they are explicitly deleted or reach their configured expiration, rather than being held only in memory during processing. Data processed via this API therefore falls outside ZDR, which is consistent with the point that stateful features step outside a ZDR arrangement.

questions.question: A content-moderation workflow sends a borderline prompt and receives a normal 200 response, but the Message's stop_reason indicates the model declined to continue rather than completing the task, and no exception was thrown anywhere in the pipeline. The team wants to know whether this is an integration bug or expected model behavior before deciding how to handle it. What is the correct interpretation?

options.label: A
options.text: This indicates a bug in the integration layer, because a 200 response with a stop_reason of model refusal should not occur, and the pipeline should be corrected to treat such responses as errors, for example by raising an exception.

options.label: B
options.text: This is expected model output behavior, not an integration failure; the pipeline should branch on this stop_reason value and handle it deliberately, such as adjusting the prompt or informing the user.

options.label: C
options.text: This indicates the API key lacks permission for the requested model tier, so the team should verify the key’s tier in the Console and request an upgrade if necessary, for example by submitting a usage tier increase request.

options.label: D
options.text: This indicates the request malformed the messages array, so the pipeline should treat it as an invalid request by returning an error to the client, for example by wrapping it in a 400 invalid_request_error response.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect. A 200 response with a stop_reason of model refusal is a legitimate API outcome and does not indicate an integration bug. The pipeline should not treat this as an error by raising an exception; instead, it should handle the stop_reason gracefully as an expected model behavior. B: Correct. This is expected model output behavior, not an integration failure. The stop_reason field is a standard part of the API response that communicates the model’s decision to decline, and the pipeline should branch on this value to handle it deliberately, such as by adjusting the prompt or informing the user. C: Incorrect. An API key lacking permission for the requested model tier would result in a 403 permission_error at the HTTP level before any Message content is returned, not a 200 response with a stop_reason. The observed behavior points to model refusal, not an authorization issue. D: Incorrect. A malformed messages array is rejected with a 400 invalid_request_error before generation occurs; it would never produce a 200 response with content and a stop_reason. Therefore, this scenario does not match the described symptoms.

questions.question: A team is deciding how to authenticate a mix of workloads: (1) a data scientist's laptop script for one-off prototyping, (2) a GitHub Actions workflow that runs on every pull request, (3) a long-running Kubernetes deployment, and (4) a single-tenant on-prem server with no OIDC-capable identity provider available. For which of these should the team select an API key rather than Workload Identity Federation as the better fit? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A
options.text: None of these; Workload Identity Federation is strictly better for every listed workload.

options.label: B
options.text: The GitHub Actions workflow that runs on every pull request.

options.label: C
options.text: The long-running Kubernetes deployment.

options.label: D
options.text: The data scientist's laptop script for one-off prototyping.

options.label: E
options.text: The single-tenant on-prem server with no OIDC-capable identity provider available.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect. The documentation explicitly recommends API keys over WIF for local development/prototyping and single-tenant servers where you control secret storage, so WIF is not strictly better across all four cases. B: Incorrect as a selection for API key preference. GitHub Actions is explicitly named as a supported WIF identity provider via its OIDC token, and CI/CD pipelines are called out as a best fit for WIF specifically to eliminate static secrets in CI. C: Incorrect as a selection for API key preference. Production workloads on cloud platforms including Kubernetes are the named best fit for WIF, since the platform already issues a workload identity that can be federated. D: Correct. API keys are documented as best for local development, prototyping, scripts, and single-tenant servers where you control secret storage; a one-off laptop script fits this exactly. E: Correct. Without an OIDC-capable identity provider, there is no federation issuer to register; an API key (with an appropriate expiration and secrets-manager storage) is the practical choice, matching the 'single-tenant servers' use case.

questions.question: A team deploying an agent that calls external tools wants to catch injection attempts embedded in tool outputs (not just user input) before Claude ever sees the raw content. Which architecture achieves this?

options.label: A
options.text: Disable all tool use in the agent and replace it with a robust, regularly updated internal knowledge base that provides pre-validated responses to user queries, since external tool outputs inherently cannot be screened for injection attempts by any technical mechanism.

options.label: B
options.text: Cache all tool outputs in a secure environment for 24 hours before use, with an automated review process during the delay that compares outputs against a blocklist of known injection patterns, since caching delays have been documented to neutralize time-sensitive injection payloads.

options.label: C
options.text: Have Claude read the raw tool output directly and rely entirely on a comprehensive set of system prompt instructions that meticulously describe injection patterns and command the model to disregard any content that fits those patterns, without any external screening or filtering.

options.label: D
options.text: Route each tool's raw output through a lightweight classifier model constrained to a structured verdict. Only pass the content into the tool_result block if the screen finds no injection attempt; otherwise, substitute a stripped summary.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect. While an internal knowledge base can be useful, disabling all tool use is an overreaction that sacrifices the agent’s core functionality. Tool output screening is technically feasible and recommended, so eliminating external calls is not the correct mitigation. B: Incorrect. Caching and delayed review do not prevent injection; they only delay exposure, and time-sensitive payloads could still execute when later consumed. There is no documented evidence that a 24-hour cache neutralizes injection attempts, and this adds unnecessary latency without meaningful security. C: Incorrect. Relying exclusively on system prompt instructions offers no dedicated screening layer; the model may still be vulnerable to sophisticated or obfuscated injection patterns. The documented best practice adds an explicit external classifier for tool outputs to provide a stronger, more reliable defense. D: Correct. This architecture implements a pre-screening layer for tool outputs, similar to input guardrails, by using a lightweight classifier to detect injection attempts. Only sanitized or safe content is passed to Claude inside the tool_result block, preventing the model from ever seeing malicious payloads.

questions.question: A background worker periodically updates a shared resource via the API and occasionally receives an HTTP 409 conflict_error response. Logs show two worker instances processing overlapping jobs at nearly the same timestamp. What does this error indicate, and what is the correct remediation?

options.label: A
options.text: The request used an outdated API version header, which triggered a conflict error; the workers should update the anthropic-version header, such as from 2023-01-01 to the latest version, and then reissue the request.

options.label: B
options.text: The request was rejected because the API is temporarily overloaded across all users, resulting in a 409 conflict error; the workers should back off and retry without changing their concurrency model to let traffic ease.

options.label: C
options.text: The request exceeded the maximum allowed request size for that endpoint, causing a 409 conflict error; the workers should split the payload into smaller chunks each before resubmitting.

options.label: D
options.text: The request conflicted with the resource's current state because it was modified concurrently; the workers should resolve the conflict by re-reading the current state and then retrying.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect. Using an outdated API version header typically leads to a 400 invalid_request_error, not a 409. Updating the anthropic-version header does not resolve the concurrent state conflict causing the actual error. B: Incorrect. Temporary API overload across all users triggers a 529 overloaded_error, not a 409. Simply backing off and retrying without modifying the concurrency model will not prevent the repeated resource conflicts from the overlapping workers. C: Incorrect. An oversized request payload results in a 413 request_too_large error, not a 409. Splitting the payload into smaller chunks does not address the underlying issue of conflicting concurrent modifications. D: Correct. The HTTP 409 conflict_error indicates that the request conflicted with the resource’s current state because it was modified concurrently. The workers should resolve the conflict by re-reading the current state and then retrying.

questions.question: A team configures their Claude Agent SDK session with permission_mode: "bypassPermissions" and allowed_tools: ["Read"], believing this restricts the agent to read-only file access for safety during an autonomous refactor. During the run, the agent successfully executes a Bash command that deletes a directory. What is the correct explanation for this outcome?

options.label: A
options.text: The deletion happened because a PreToolUse hook was missing, and hooks are the only mechanism capable of blocking destructive Bash commands in bypass mode.

options.label: B
options.text: The team's configuration contains a syntax error, since allowed_tools cannot be combined with bypassPermissions in the same session and the SDK should have rejected it at startup.

options.label: C
options.text: allowed_tools only pre-approves the tools listed; unlisted tools like Bash are not matched by any allow rule and fall through to the permission mode, where bypassPermissions approves them anyway.

options.label: D
options.text: bypassPermissions only applies to tools explicitly named in allowed_tools, so Bash should have been blocked; this indicates a bug in the SDK's permission evaluator.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect. While a PreToolUse hook could have blocked this, hooks are not the only mechanism; using disallowed_tools to remove Bash entirely, or avoiding bypassPermissions, would also have prevented it. B: Incorrect. This combination is valid syntax and a documented (if dangerous) configuration; the SDK does not reject it. C: Correct. allowed_tools does not constrain bypassPermissions: it only pre-approves listed tools, and any tool not covered by an allow or deny rule still falls through to the permission mode step, where bypass mode approves everything. D: Incorrect. This is the inverse of the actual behavior: bypassPermissions approves tools regardless of allowed_tools, not only the ones listed in it, so nothing here indicates a bug.

questions.question: A backend engineer needs to build automation that provisions brand-new Claude API keys programmatically as part of a CI pipeline for spinning up ephemeral test environments. They plan to call an Admin API endpoint to mint each key. What will happen when they attempt this?

options.label: A
options.text: The request will fail, because the Admin API can manage existing API keys (listing, renaming, deactivating) but cannot create new ones; keys can only be created through the Claude Console.

options.label: B
options.text: The request will succeed only if the caller authenticates with an org:admin OAuth token instead of an Admin API key, because the Admin API key lacks the workspace.key.create scope needed for key creation.

options.label: C
options.text: The request will succeed and return a new key whose secret value is included exactly once in the response body, matching standard Admin API key creation behavior where the full secret is disclosed only at creation time.

options.label: D
options.text: The request will succeed but the newly created key will be inactive by default, requiring a separate Console action to activate it before first use, because keys created through the Admin API start in a disabled state.

questions.explanation: A: Correct. The Admin API only supports management of existing API keys (e.g., listing, renaming, deactivating) and does not provide an endpoint for creating new keys. New API keys can only be generated through the Claude Console, so attempting to mint keys via the Admin API will fail. B: Incorrect. The inability to create keys is not due to authentication scope limitations; regardless of whether an Admin API key or OAuth token is used, the Admin API simply does not support key creation. This operation is exclusively performed via the Claude Console. C: Incorrect. There is no Admin API endpoint for key creation, so no response body containing a secret value is ever returned. The described behavior of disclosing a secret at creation time does not apply because the creation call itself is not available. D: Incorrect. Keys cannot be created through the Admin API, so the scenario of a newly created key being inactive by default is not applicable. All key creation is done via the Claude Console, where keys are typically active upon creation unless otherwise specified.

questions.question: A team ships a Claude-powered pricing assistant whose system prompt embeds proprietary discount rules and a bearer token for an internal quotes API. Red-teamers keep extracting the prompt text with role-play requests. Which measures reduce the leakage impact? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A
options.text: Run each response through an output filter that blocks or redacts text copying long verbatim stretches of the system prompt before the user sees it.

options.label: B
options.text: Expand the system prompt with more detailed instructions around the discount rules, so extraction attempts need longer role-play sequences to succeed.

options.label: C
options.text: Lower the sampling temperature to 0 so Claude handles role-play requests about its instructions consistently instead of varying between replies.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the bearer token out of the system prompt into server-side tool code that attaches it to the internal quotes API call when Claude requests a quote.

options.label: E
options.text: Fetch the bearer token from a secrets manager at request time and render it into the system prompt template that is sent with each call to the Claude API.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: an output filter inspects each response after generation and stops verbatim reproduction of the prompt before it reaches the user. It works even when the model has been talked into complying with an extraction request. B: Incorrect: a longer prompt gives the red-teamers more proprietary material to extract, and extra instructions do not stop role-play requests from drawing the text out. Sensitive detail should be kept out of the prompt rather than added to it. C: Incorrect: temperature controls how much the sampled wording varies and does not govern what the model is willing to reveal. Role-play requests still pull out the prompt text, and a fixed setting makes the same extraction repeatable. D: Correct: when the credential lives in server-side tool code, the model never receives it, so prompting cannot extract it and a leaked prompt exposes no working secret. E: Incorrect: a secrets manager changes where the token is stored, but the value is inserted into the prompt template, so the model still receives it. A role-play extraction would reveal the live credential in the response.

questions.question: A production engineering team just received a deprecation notice for a model powering a customer-facing workflow, with a retirement date several months away. Which of the following are best practices Anthropic recommends for handling this situation? (Select all that apply.)

options.label: A
options.text: Disable the anthropic-version header on all requests, since deprecated models bypass normal API versioning rules until they are retired.

options.label: B
options.text: Wait until the exact retirement date to make any code changes, since requests to deprecated models continue working normally until that date.

options.label: C
options.text: Test the application thoroughly against the recommended replacement model well before the retirement date, rather than waiting until the deadline.

options.label: D
options.text: Ignore the deprecation notice unless the application's error rate visibly increases, since deprecated models behave identically to active ones.

options.label: E
options.text: Update the application to the recommended replacement model as soon as practical, rather than continuing to run on the deprecated model until forced.

options.label: F
options.text: Export usage data from the Claude Console Usage page to confirm exactly where the deprecated model is still being called in production.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect -- there is no mechanism where deprecated models bypass API versioning, and the anthropic-version header should never be disabled; it's unrelated to a model's deprecation status. B: Incorrect -- while deprecated models do keep working until retirement, waiting until the deadline to act contradicts Anthropic's recommendation to test and migrate well in advance. C: Correct -- Anthropic's stated best practice is to test applications with newer models well before the retirement date, not to wait until the deadline. D: Incorrect -- deprecated models are explicitly called out as likely to be less reliable than active models, so treating them as behaviorally identical and waiting for visible errors contradicts Anthropic's guidance. E: Correct -- Anthropic recommends updating to the recommended replacement as soon as practical rather than continuing on the deprecated model until forced to migrate. F: Correct -- exporting the Usage page CSV is the recommended way to locate every instance where a deprecated model is still being called.

questions.question: A security review requires that a specific check run on every single tool call Claude makes, regardless of which permission mode is active or which allow rules match. Which mechanism satisfies this requirement?

options.label: A
options.text: The canUseTool callback is invoked on every tool call and applies its evaluation logic regardless of the active permission mode, ensuring the check runs each time.

options.label: B
options.text: The acceptEdits permission mode inspects each file operation individually and applies the inspection check regardless of the active permission mode, so it runs on every tool call.

options.label: C
options.text: An allowed_tools entry for each tool ensures that every tool call is verified against the check in all permission modes, including bypassPermissions.

options.label: D
options.text: A PreToolUse hook runs before every permission check and its denial works in bypassPermissions mode, so it can enforce the check on every tool call.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect. The canUseTool callback is not invoked for calls that are resolved by hooks, deny rules, permission mode (including bypassPermissions), or allow rules. Only a small subset of calls reach it, so it cannot ensure a check on every tool call. B: Incorrect. The acceptEdits permission mode only auto-approves file operations that match its patterns, without running a custom inspection. Moreover, it does not apply to non-file tool calls, so it cannot enforce a check on every tool call. C: Incorrect. An allowed_tools entry simply pre-approves a tool without running a custom check; moreover, in bypassPermissions mode, all tools are allowed without any check, so it does not enforce verification on every call. D: Correct. A PreToolUse hook runs before any permission evaluation, and its denial takes effect even in bypassPermissions mode, so it can enforce a check on every tool call unconditionally.

questions.question: A workspace administrator needs to give a new engineer the ability to add and remove members within a single workspace, but that engineer should not be able to view or modify billing information or manage other workspaces in the organization. Which access pattern satisfies least privilege here?

options.label: A
options.text: Assign the engineer the organization-level billing role to manage workspace membership, because billing privileges include the ability to modify workspace members lists through the organization billing endpoint.

options.label: B
options.text: Assign the engineer a workspace-scoped role (such as workspace_admin) limited to that single workspace via the workspace members endpoint. Avoid an organization-level admin or billing role.

options.label: C
options.text: Assign the engineer the organization-level admin role to manage workspace membership; this role grants add/remove member permissions across all workspaces in the organization through the organization members endpoint.

options.label: D
options.text: Create a shared Admin API key for the workspace and have the engineer use it to call the workspace members endpoint for adding and removing members, since Admin API keys are automatically scoped per workspace.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect. The billing role is designed for managing billing information, not workspace membership. It does not grant permissions to add or remove members from a workspace. B: Correct. Assigning a workspace-scoped role like workspace_admin via the workspace members endpoint limits the engineer to managing membership within that single workspace, aligning with the principle of least privilege. This avoids granting unnecessary organization-level admin or billing permissions. C: Incorrect. Organization-level admin grants broad permissions, including user management across the entire organization, which exceeds the single-workspace scope needed. This violates the principle of least privilege. D: Incorrect. Admin API keys are associated with organization-level credentials and are not automatically scoped to a single workspace. Sharing a key also violates security best practices and least privilege, as it grants more access than necessary.

questions.question: A company is building a support chatbot on the Agent SDK. It should not present itself as Claude Code, needs a distinct persona and name, and runs unattended with a narrow, pre-approved tool surface rather than a human approving each step. Which system prompt approach best fits this product?

options.label: A
options.text: Write a custom system prompt that defines the bot's identity, scope, and needed tool-usage and safety guidance, since the product's surface and permission model differs from Claude Code's default.

options.label: B
options.text: Leave systemPrompt unset and convey the bot’s persona, tool restrictions, and safety constraints through the first user message of each unattended session while relying on the SDK’s default system prompt for basic agent behavior.

options.label: C
options.text: Load an output style file that sets keep-coding-instructions: true to preserve Claude Code's engineering guidance while adding a support persona, so the bot maintains reliable tool-use patterns alongside its customer-facing role.

options.label: D
options.text: Use the claude_code preset with append text describing a distinct persona and restricted tool set, since the preset provides reliable scaffolding while appending product-specific limitations.

questions.explanation: A: Correct. A custom system prompt is the best approach because the bot requires a distinct identity, scope, and tool surface that differ significantly from the Claude Code defaults. The Claude Code preset assumes a human-in-the-loop coding tool, which is inappropriate for an unattended support bot with a different persona and narrow tool permissions. B: Incorrect. Leaving systemPrompt unset means the SDK uses a minimal default that lacks any support-bot persona, scope, or safety instructions. Conveying these critical details through the first user message is unreliable and would need to be repeated every session, failing to establish the persistent, unattended behavior the product requires. C: Incorrect. Setting keep-coding-instructions: true preserves Claude Code's engineering guidance, which is designed for coding tasks and conflicts with the bot's customer-support purpose. This approach fails to remove the coding-tool persona and would instead inject irrelevant instructions, undermining the distinct support identity required. D: Incorrect. Using append with the claude_code preset retains the underlying coding-tool persona and safety framing, which contradicts the requirement that the bot not present itself as Claude Code. Appending custom instructions cannot override or replace the preset's ingrained identity and tool-usage patterns, making this approach unsuitable for a support bot with different branding and scope.

questions.question: A platform team runs thousands of Agent SDK sessions across many developers' machines and repository checkouts. Every session uses the same claude_code preset with the same append text, yet nearly every session misses the prompt cache. Investigation shows the preset places a per-user value, the auto memory directory location derived from each repository's path on disk, in the system prompt ahead of the append text. The team wants identical configurations to share one cached system prompt, wants to keep the preset's tool and safety guidance, and accepts that per-user context may reach Claude through the conversation instead. What should they do?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch the system prompt's cache duration from five minutes to one hour, so a later session can reuse a cache entry that an earlier session wrote even though the prompt text differs.

options.label: B
options.text: Replace the preset with a custom system prompt string that contains the same append text, so the SDK sends only that string and the preset's per-user value is removed from the prompt.

options.label: C
options.text: Turn on the preset's exclude-dynamic-sections option (excludeDynamicSections in TypeScript), moving per-user context into the first user message so the system prompt stays static.

options.label: D
options.text: Move the shared append text into a CLAUDE.md file, because CLAUDE.md content is delivered in the conversation, so the system prompt no longer needs any customization to be cached.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect. A longer cache duration only keeps an entry alive for longer; it does not make different prompts match. Cache hits require identical prompt segments up to the cache breakpoint, so sessions whose system prompts contain different per-user values still cannot read each other's entries, and the longer duration only raises the cost of cache writes. B: Incorrect. A custom string would drop the per-user value, but it also replaces the whole preset, and the SDK then sends only what the team writes. The team would lose the preset's tool-usage and safety guidance and would have to rewrite it, which the scenario says it wants to keep; the preset's own option for excluding dynamic sections achieves the cache sharing without that loss. C: Correct. The claude_code preset places a per-user value, the auto memory directory location derived from the repository's path on disk, in the system prompt ahead of the append text, so sessions on different machines and checkouts never share a cache entry. Enabling the exclude-dynamic-sections option moves that per-user context into the first user message, leaving only the static preset and append text in the system prompt so identical configurations share one cached entry. The trade-off is that instructions in a user message carry marginally less weight than the same text in the system prompt. D: Incorrect. The preset still builds its own system prompt and still embeds the per-user memory location ahead of any customization, so the system prompt continues to differ across sessions. CLAUDE.md content already reaches Claude in the conversation rather than the system prompt, so relocating the shared text there does not change the part of the prompt that is breaking cache matching.

questions.question: A team is choosing infrastructure for a long-running, asynchronous production agent and does not want to operate its own sandbox or session-state infrastructure, while another team wants an agent that works directly against files on its own servers using a Python library. Which statement correctly matches a team's need to the right approach?

options.label: A
options.text: The team avoiding sandbox operations should use the Agent SDK, since it stores session state as an Anthropic-hosted event log rather than local JSONL files

options.label: B
options.text: Both teams should use the Agent SDK, since Managed Agents cannot be reached through a REST API and requires the team to host their own sandbox

options.label: C
options.text: The team that does not want to operate its own sandbox or session-state infrastructure should use Managed Agents, though the team must still implement its own prompt caching and context compaction since Managed Agents does not provide those optimizations

options.label: D
options.text: The team working directly against files on its own servers using a Python library should use the Agent SDK, which runs inside its own process

options.label: E
options.text: The team working directly against local files should use Managed Agents, since Managed Agents execute directly on the customer's own infrastructure by default

questions.explanation: A: This is incorrect. The team that wants to avoid operating sandbox and session-state infrastructure should use Managed Agents, not the Agent SDK. The Agent SDK runs the agent loop in the team's own process and is not described as offloading session state to an Anthropic-hosted event log. B: This is incorrect. Managed Agents is a hosted REST API where Anthropic runs the agent and sandbox; it does not require the team to host its own sandbox. The first team should use Managed Agents, while the second team should use the Agent SDK — not both. C: This is incorrect. The team that does not want to operate its own sandbox or session-state infrastructure is correctly matched to Managed Agents, but the claim about prompt caching and compaction is false: Managed Agents' harness includes built-in prompt caching and context compaction as part of the managed infrastructure, so the team does not need to build these optimizations itself. D: Correct. The Claude Agent SDK provides the same tools, agent loop, and context management as Claude Code, but runs the agent loop inside the developer's own process. This makes it appropriate for teams that need to work directly against files on their own servers using a Python library, including CI/CD and local execution. E: This is incorrect. Managed Agents is Anthropic-hosted and does not execute directly on the customer's own infrastructure by default. A team working directly against local files on its own servers should use the Agent SDK, which runs the agent loop inside the team's own process.

questions.question: A team is building a single codebase that must call Claude through both the direct Anthropic API and Amazon Bedrock, and their images are currently referenced by public HTTPS URLs to avoid re-uploading binary data. What must change for the Bedrock code path?

options.label: A
options.text: Host the images on an AWS-owned domain instead of a third-party URL, since Bedrock's url source type only resolves URLs within the same AWS account

options.label: B
options.text: Nothing needs to change, since Bedrock supports the identical url source type as the direct Anthropic API for all image content blocks

options.label: C
options.text: Convert image sources to base64-encoded data for the Bedrock path, since Amazon Bedrock currently accepts only base64-encoded image sources

options.label: D
options.text: Switch to the Files API and pass a file_id for the Bedrock path, since Bedrock only accepts file references and never accepts inline image data

questions.explanation: A: There's no documented AWS-domain exception for the url source type on Bedrock; the limitation is that URL sources aren't supported at all on Bedrock, regardless of hosting location. B: URL-based image sources are not currently available on Bedrock; this directly contradicts the documented platform limitation. C: Correct. The Vision documentation states that on Amazon Bedrock only base64-encoded image sources are available, so URL-based image references must be converted to base64 for the Bedrock code path. D: The Files API and its file_id references are part of the direct Claude API's feature set; Bedrock's supported source type for images is base64, not file references.
